nameStory: Baby's-breath gets its charming name from those delicate clouds of tiny white flowers that look as soft and airy as a baby's gentle breath. But there's a less romantic origin story too – some say the name comes from the plant's distinctive scent, which has been described as smelling like sour milk or baby spit-up!
description: Baby's-breath is a bushy perennial plant that creates stunning clouds of tiny white flowers in summer. It grows into a rounded mound about 4 feet tall and wide, with many branching stems that become completely covered in thousands of small blooms. Originally from Europe, this plant has made itself at home in parts of New England, though it's not commonly encountered here. The overall effect is like a soft, white cloud sitting in the landscape.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Countless tiny white flowers, each only about 1/8 inch across, cluster together in airy, cloud-like masses that seem to float above the foliage

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a bushy, rounded mound with many thin, branching stems that spread outward and upward, creating a dome-shaped plant

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves that feel somewhat thick and waxy to the touch, arranged in opposite pairs along the stems

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thin, wiry stems that branch repeatedly, feeling smooth and slightly swollen at the joints where leaves attach

idTips.label: Scent
idTips.description: Has a distinctive sour, milky odor when crushed or bruised – not the sweet fragrance you might expect from such delicate flowers

habitat: Look for baby's-breath in dry, sandy, or rocky areas with good drainage, especially where the soil is alkaline or chalky. In New England, you're most likely to find it in disturbed areas, old gardens, or places where it has escaped cultivation. It prefers full sun and doesn't tolerate wet or boggy conditions.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as small rosettes of narrow leaves, with stems beginning to branch and elongate as the weather warms.
seasonality.summer: Peak bloom time when the entire plant becomes a spectacular cloud of tiny white flowers, making it unmistakable in the landscape.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and the plant begins to look scraggly, with dried flower heads persisting and seeds dispersing on the wind.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level in harsh winters, leaving dried stems that may persist until broken by snow and wind.

funFact: Baby's-breath is sometimes called 'chalk-loving' plant because its scientific name Gypsophila literally means 'lover of gypsum' – it actually thrives in soils that would be too alkaline for most other plants to survive!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other small white wildflowers, but no other plant creates such massive, airy clouds of tiny blooms. Queen Anne's lace has flat-topped flower clusters, while baby's-breath forms rounded, three-dimensional puffs of flowers.
contextualKnowledge: This is primarily a garden plant that occasionally escapes cultivation – you're much more likely to see it at a florist shop than in the wild in New England. It's widely used in flower arrangements because the dried flowers last for months.
compareHints: Baby's-breath differs from its relatives like cowherb by forming much larger, bushier plants with more extensively branched flower clusters. While cowherb stays closer to the ground with simpler flower arrangements, baby's-breath creates those characteristic billowing clouds of blooms that make it instantly recognizable.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Gypsophila relatives in New England, cowherb is unique for its blue-gray waxy appearance and pale pink flowers.
Showy baby's-breath differs from regular baby's-breath by being an annual (lives one season) rather than perennial, and having larger, showier individual flowers.
Unlike common baby's-breath which has smooth stems and grows into large perennial clumps, glandular baby's-breath is an annual with distinctly sticky, glandular stems.
